subject: Chemistry
topic: Periodic table trends II — mixed tiers
description: Atomic radius, ionisation energy, electronegativity, electron affinity across periods/groups

questions.stem: Across a PERIOD of the periodic table from left to right, the ATOMIC RADIUS generally:

options.option_text: Increases due to addition of one outer shell of electrons
Decreases due to higher nuclear charge pulling electrons closer
Stays the same with no significant trend at all
Fluctuates randomly with no observable systematic pattern

questions.explanation: Across a period: protons added in the nucleus, electrons added in the SAME shell. The increasing nuclear charge pulls the electron cloud INWARD → ATOMIC RADIUS DECREASES from Li to Ne, Na to Ar, etc. Down a GROUP: each new shell adds → atomic radius INCREASES (Li < Na < K < Rb < Cs). Distractor 1 describes group-trend, not period. Distractor 3, 4 are wrong as the trend is systematic.

questions.stem: IONISATION ENERGY is the energy needed to:

options.option_text: Combine an atom with another atom to form a covalent bond
Remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom
Add one electron to a gaseous atom from its surroundings
Break the strongest covalent bond in a small molecule

questions.explanation: First ionisation energy (IE₁) — energy to remove the outermost electron from a neutral GASEOUS atom: M(g) → M⁺(g) + e⁻. Increases across a period (harder to remove e⁻ as nuclear pull grows); decreases down a group (outer e⁻ farther from nucleus, easier to remove). Highest IE₁: helium (2372 kJ/mol). Lowest: caesium (~376) and francium. Successive ionisation energies (IE₂, IE₃, ...) are progressively higher. Distractor 1 = bond formation. Distractor 3 = electron AFFINITY. Distractor 4 = bond dissociation energy.

questions.stem: ELECTRONEGATIVITY measures the tendency of an atom to:

options.option_text: Lose electrons easily to form a positive ion
Attract shared electrons in a chemical bond
Emit a photon of visible light when heated
Combine with hydrogen to form a stable hydride

questions.explanation: Electronegativity (χ) — relative tendency to attract bonding electrons toward itself. Pauling scale: F (3.98, highest) > O > N > Cl > Br > C > H. Cs/Fr (0.7-0.8, lowest among stable elements). Periodic trends: increases across a period (toward F), decreases down a group. ΔEN between two atoms predicts bond ionicity: > 1.7 mostly ionic; 0.4-1.7 polar covalent; < 0.4 non-polar covalent. Distractor 1 = electropositivity (opposite). Distractor 3 = unrelated optical property. Distractor 4 = some elements form hydrides but that's not electronegativity.

questions.stem: Which element has the HIGHEST electronegativity on the Pauling scale?

options.option_text: Oxygen, the most abundant element by mass
Fluorine, the most reactive halogen of all
Chlorine, found mostly as common rock salt
Nitrogen, the most abundant gas in air around us

questions.explanation: Pauling electronegativity ranking: F (3.98) > O (3.44) > Cl (3.16) > N (3.04) > Br (2.96) > I (2.66) > C (2.55) > H (2.20) > Cs/Fr (~0.7). Fluorine is the most electronegative because of small atomic size + high effective nuclear charge. Drives its extreme reactivity (forms compounds with nearly every other element). Distractor 1 — oxygen is 2nd, not 1st. Distractor 3 — chlorine 3rd. Distractor 4 — nitrogen 4th.

questions.stem: ELECTRON AFFINITY of an atom is:

options.option_text: The energy needed to remove its outermost electron
The energy released when an electron is added to it
The number of valence electrons it carries naturally
Its tendency to share electrons within a bond

questions.explanation: Electron Affinity (EA) — energy released when one electron is added to a neutral gaseous atom: X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g) + EA. Halogens have the highest EAs (Cl ~349 kJ/mol, F ~328, Br ~325) — eager to gain e⁻ to complete octet. Group 18 (noble gases) and group 2 (alkaline earth) have ~0 or negative EA. EA is RELATED but different from electronegativity (which is a derived ratio). Distractor 1 = ionisation energy. Distractor 3 = valence count. Distractor 4 = electronegativity.

questions.stem: Going DOWN a group of the periodic table, which property generally INCREASES?

options.option_text: First ionisation energy of the elements
Atomic radius and metallic character of the elements
Electronegativity of the elements involved
Effective nuclear charge felt by valence electrons

questions.explanation: Down a group: more inner shells → larger atomic radius. Outer e⁻ are farther from nucleus → less tightly held → easier to lose → MORE METALLIC. Examples: Group 1 — Li (least metallic) → Cs (most metallic among stable, very reactive); Group 14 — C (non-metal), Si (metalloid), Ge (metalloid), Sn/Pb (metals). Distractor 1 — IE DECREASES down a group. Distractor 3 — electronegativity DECREASES. Distractor 4 — effective nuclear charge stays roughly similar (more shielding).

questions.stem: The MOST METALLIC element among Li, Na, K, Cs is:

options.option_text: Lithium, the topmost in the alkali group
Caesium, the heaviest stable alkali metal
Sodium, the second member of the group
Potassium, in the middle of this group

questions.explanation: Metallic character INCREASES down a group. Cs (caesium) is the most metallic among stable alkali metals — most reactive (Fr is more so but radioactive + scarce). Caesium is so reactive it ignites instantly in air, reacts explosively with water. It is a soft, golden metal that melts in your hand (mp ~28 °C). Used in atomic clocks (the SI second is defined by Cs-133 transition), photoelectric cells, ion-propulsion thrusters.
